transcript.text: There's water all over the kitchen floor coming from under my Beko washing machine and its gone under the units to where the plug is, the machine is still going. What do I do?

Water near the plug or socket is dangerous. Please don't touch the plug, socket or machine if they or your hands are wet. If you can do it safely, switch off the circuit at the consumer unit (fuse box), keep away from the water, and don't use the machine again until a qualified electrician or appliance engineer has checked it. 1. Switch the power off at the consumer unit (fuse box), on the circuit for the kitchen sockets, or the main switch if you're not sure which one. Don't touch the plug, socket or machine while there's water around them. Turning the power off this way stops the machine safely.
2. Turn off the water supply to the machine. This is usually a small tap with a blue or lever handle on the pipe behind or beside it, often under the sink. That stops any more water coming in.
3. Mop up with towels, starting from the side away from the socket. Leave the door shut, because the drum may still be full of water and opening it would add to the flood.
4. Leave the power off to that circuit. Because water has reached the socket, the machine and that socket mustn't be used again until a qualified engineer or electrician has checked them. 1. The pump filter cap at the bottom front isn't screwed in fully, or its rubber seal is dirty or damaged. This is very common if the filter has been cleaned recently.
2. An internal hose has split or worked loose, usually the sump hose between the drum and the pump, or the drain pump housing itself is leaking. This usually shows up while it's washing or draining.
3. Water is escaping at the front through a damaged door seal, or out of the detergent drawer. Too much detergent, or one that isn't low-foam, can make the machine foam over.
4. Less often, a loose drain or fill hose connection at the back is to blame. 1. Has the pump filter been opened recently? If so, the cap or its seal is the first suspect.
2. Look at the door seal folds and the detergent drawer area for suds or wet tracks. Foam or a wet drawer area points to detergent or the drawer. A dry front points underneath, to the pump, filter or hoses.
3. Has the machine been moved or reconnected recently? If so, the hose connections at the back are more likely. The answer that would narrow it down most is in my question below. Dark, greasy water would suggest a more serious internal problem than a hose or filter.
ok I'm going to the fuse box now, I'm in socks on the wet floor though. should I take them off or is it ok? the machine is still running

Take the wet socks off or swap them for dry shoes. Wet socks conduct and give you no protection, and dry rubber-soled shoes, slippers or wellies are much better. Dry your hands too before you touch the fuse box. 1. Don't walk through the water, especially near the machine or that socket. Go round it if you can.
2. At the consumer unit, stand on a dry floor with dry hands. Flip the switch for the kitchen sockets, or the main switch if you're not sure which one. That will stop the machine. You don't need to go near it.
3. If the consumer unit is wet or sparking, or you'd have to stand in water to reach it, leave it alone. Stay out of the kitchen and call an emergency electrician. Cutting the power at the board is the safe way to stop it, and a bit more water on the floor matters far less than you staying safe. Once the power is off and the water tap to the machine is shut, the mopping up can wait a few minutes. Then we can work out where it's leaking from. Whatever the cause turns out to be, the machine and that socket need checking by an engineer or electrician before they're used again, because water reached the socket.
ok I've taken my socks off, the hall floor is dry so I can reach the fuse box fine. do I just flip the kitchen sockets switch or the main one? I'm not sure which is which

Flip the main switch. If you're not sure which one is the kitchen sockets, the main switch is the right choice because it most likely cuts power to everything, including that socket and the machine. It's usually the large switch at one end of the board, often red or labelled 'Main switch' or 'Mains isolator'. 1. 2. Push the main switch to OFF. The machine should stop straight away. You don't need to go anywhere near it.
3. If the labels aren't clear, just leave the main off for now. A fridge-freezer will be fine for a few hours if you keep its doors shut.
4. If one of the switches has already dropped to OFF by itself, the water has probably tripped it. Leave it off and don't reset it. Next, turn off the water tap to the machine and mop from the side away from the socket. The machine and that socket must stay off until an engineer or electrician has checked them, whatever is causing the leak. When it's safe, have a look at the water on the floor: is it clean, soapy, or dark and greasy? That tells us a lot about where it's coming from.
[Safety panel] An appliance that keeps tripping your electrics — or that smells of burning or has scorch marks — may have an electrical fault. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it, don't keep resetting it, and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer.
ok main switch it is, flipping it now. it's off and the machine has stopped. the water by the plug is clear I think, not soapy or dark. what now?

Well done, that was the important bit. With the power off you're safe to deal with the water now. 1. Turn off the water tap to the machine, if you haven't yet, so nothing more can come in.
2. Mop up with towels, working from the side away from the socket. Don't touch the plug or socket, and don't open the door or the pump filter yet. There's probably still water in the drum, and opening either would put it on the floor.
3. Leave the main switch off for now. Before the socket is used again it needs checking by an electrician, and the machine must not be used again until an engineer has looked at it. It makes a failed drum bearing unlikely, because that usually leaks dark, greasy water. It points to the water side of the machine. 1. The pump filter cap at the bottom front not being fully tight, or its seal leaking.
2. An internal hose (often the sump hose under the drum) or the drain pump housing leaking.
3. The fill side: the hose connection at the back or the inlet valve. Clean incoming water fits this one quite well. 1. Look at the filter cap without opening it. If it's sitting crooked or not screwed fully home, or has drips on it, that's the most likely source. Did anyone clean the filter recently?
2. Pull the machine out only if it moves easily, and only if the area round the socket is dry. Look at the hose where it joins the back of the machine and the tap. A wet connection or a dripping washer points to the fill hose.
3. Look round the door seal folds and the detergent drawer. Dry and clean there points away from the front and towards something underneath. An engineer will be able to pin it down faster if you can tell them where and when it leaked, which is what my question below is about.
[Safety panel] An appliance that keeps tripping your electrics — or that smells of burning or has scorch marks — may have an electrical fault. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it, don't keep resetting it, and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer.
ok power's off and I'll do the towels. the water seems to be mostly coming from the front under the door. should I check anything else or is it just wait for an engineer?

You'll need an engineer either way. Water reached the socket, so the machine mustn't be used again until it's been checked, and the socket needs an electrician too. But a couple of quick look-only checks, with the main switch still off, will help the engineer find it faster and might show it's something simple. Clear water coming from the front under the door narrows it down. 1. The pump filter cap, usually behind a small flap at the bottom front. If it isn't fully tight, or its seal is dirty or worn, it leaks clean water straight out at the front.
2. The bottom of the door seal. A split hidden in the folds, or a coin or underwire holding it open, lets water out under the door.
3. Less likely, water running down the front from the detergent drawer, or too much detergent foaming over. This is less likely. 1. Dry the front of the machine and the floor right in front of it with a towel, then watch for a few minutes. If it keeps dripping with the machine off, the water is coming from something that's still holding water, which points to the filter cap or the bottom of the door seal.
2. Open the little flap at the bottom front, if your machine has one, but don't unscrew the filter. Is the cap crooked, or wet and dripping around its edge? If so, the cap or its seal is the likely source.
3. Look down the front panel below the detergent drawer. A wet streak or soap residue running down from the drawer points to the drawer, not the door. If none of those shows anything, the door seal or something just inside the front is the most likely cause, and the engineer can check the seal and drain the drum safely. Tell them it was clear water at the front under the door, and what stage the wash had reached, if you know.
ok I've dried the front and looked at the door seal, there's a small split in the bottom fold and a bra underwire stuck right next to it. is that the cause?

Yes, that's probably it. A split in the bottom fold of the door seal is exactly where water collects during a wash, and an underwire trapped beside it is the classic way a seal gets punctured. That fits everything you've described: clear water coming out at the front, under the door. 1. Pull the underwire out gently, if it comes free easily. Don't force it, because that could tear the split further. If it's poking through one of the drum holes, it may have more length behind it. In that case leave it for the engineer, as underwires often end up in the pump or sump too.
2. If the door is open, gently lift the front edge of the drum and push it down. A little movement is normal. A lot of up-and-down play, or a clunk, would suggest the drum bearings are worn and could be rubbing the seal. That needs fixing first, or a new seal would get damaged as well.
3. Don't try to tape or glue the split. Seal repairs don't hold under wash pressure. It still needs an engineer before it's used again, because water reached the socket. When you book, tell them it's a split door seal with an underwire found next to it, clear water leaking at the front, and that the drum may still have water in it. They can then drain it safely, bring a seal that fits your model, and check the drum and pump for any more wire. Have the socket checked by an electrician too. A door seal is normally a reasonable repair on a machine that's otherwise in good condition, so it's usually worth fixing rather than replacing the machine. A wash bag for underwired bras would help stop it happening again.
